overview:
Sthanakavasi practice refers to the lived religious, ethical, and communal life of the Śvetāmbara Sthānakavāsī Jains, a non‑idolatrous sub‑tradition that crystallized in western India in the 17th century. The term "Sthānakavāsī" literally means "one who dwells or assembles in a meeting‑hall (sthanak)", indicating their preference for simple prayer halls rather than ornate temples with images. Historically rooted in the reformist insights of the 15th‑century lay scholar Loṅkā Śāh and institutionalized by Lava (Lavjī Rishi) of Surat, Sthanakavasi practice is defined by a combination of scriptural fidelity, rigorous ascetic discipline, and an emphasis on inner worship (bhāva‑pūjā) over external image‑worship. They accept thirty‑two Śvetāmbara Āgamas as authoritative and argue that these canonical texts do not prescribe idol construction or temple ritual, so they regard such practices as later accretions that can distract from the core Jain path of non‑violence, right faith, right knowledge, and right conduct.

At the heart of Sthanakavasi practice is a strong focus on ahiṃsā (non‑violence) in thought, speech, and action. This is visible most clearly in the lifestyle of their mendicants, who wear simple white robes, carry very few possessions, and cover their mouths with a square white cloth (muhapatti) to reduce the risk of inhaling small insects. Monks and nuns take the great vows (mahāvratas) of non‑violence, truthfulness, non‑stealing, celibacy, and non‑attachment, and their daily routine is carefully regulated to support these vows. They eat only between sunrise and sunset, take food as alms from lay followers, do not store food or water overnight, and avoid staying in one place for long periods except during the monsoon retreat (cāturmāsa). These disciplines are understood not merely as external rules but as continuous training in vigilance (samiti) and restraint (gupti), cultivating equanimity and awareness of the countless living beings that share the world.

Lay Sthanakavasi practice mirrors this ascetic ethos in moderated form. Household Jains undertake anuvratas (small vows) corresponding to the monastic mahāvratas, adopt vegetarianism, and often observe additional dietary and behavioral restraints to minimize harm. Regular pratikramaṇa (ritual confession and reflection), svādhyāya (scriptural study), and meditation sessions are central to community life and typically take place in the sthanak meeting‑halls rather than in image‑filled temples. In these halls, the focus is on recitation of canonical texts, ethical discourses by monks and nuns, and collective reflection on karma, right conduct, and the stages of spiritual development (gunasthāna). Mental worship—cultivating reverence for the Tīrthaṅkaras through contemplation of their qualities, rather than through physical images—is emphasized as the most authentic way to honor enlightened beings.

Sthanakavasi practice also has a distinctive social and institutional dimension. The community is sometimes known as Dhundhiya ("searchers") or Sādhumārgi ("followers of sadhus"), highlighting their orientation toward seeking truth through disciplined renunciation and scriptural inquiry. Their mendicant orders are organized around lineages of teachers who stress strict observance of vows and simplicity of life, and historically they were known for choosing secluded or neglected buildings as residences to avoid disturbing others and to maintain focus on spiritual pursuits. From within the Sthanakavasi stream, the Terāpanth order emerged in the 18th century under Ācārya Bhikṣu, further systematizing ascetic discipline while retaining the non‑idolatrous stance. In contemporary practice, Sthanakavasi communities are prominent in Gujarat, Rajasthan, Punjab, and parts of Maharashtra, and many adherents identify themselves as "Śvetāmbara Sthānakavāsī", signaling continuity with the broader Śvetāmbara tradition alongside their particular reforms.

Doctrinally, Sthanakavasi practice aligns closely with mainstream Śvetāmbara Jainism on core philosophical points—such as the nature of the soul (jīva), the structure of the universe, the theory of karma, and the path to liberation—while differing primarily on the role of images and temples. They maintain that the Tīrthaṅkaras are best approached through internal transformation and adherence to vows, not through material offerings or elaborate rituals that may involve subtle forms of harm (for example, cutting flowers or burning incense). Scriptural study is therefore not a peripheral activity but a central religious duty, and many Sthanakavasi teachers have been respected for their mastery of Prakrit and Sanskrit Jain texts. In everyday life, this translates into a culture where ethical discipline, humility, and service are prioritized over architectural or ritual display.

Modern Sthanakavasi practice continues to negotiate questions of tradition and change. Urbanization, education, and global migration have led to new forms of sthanak‑style meeting halls, including multi‑purpose community centers and digital platforms for svādhyāya and discourse. At the same time, the core commitments—to non‑violence, simplicity, scriptural grounding, and inner worship—remain the touchstones by which practices are evaluated. While Sthanakavasi Jains do not claim exclusive access to truth, they see their non‑idolatrous path as a faithful application of Mahāvīra’s teachings in a way that minimizes harm and keeps attention on the transformation of the practitioner rather than on external objects of devotion.

primary_sources.title: Ācārāṅga Sūtra (Acaranga Sutra)
primary_sources.author: Traditionally attributed to disciples of Mahāvīra within the Śvetāmbara canon
primary_sources.original_text:
सव्वे पाणा न हन्तव्वा, न लिंहव्वा न बन्धव्वा।
एसा धम्मो महाविरो, अहिंसा परमं व्रतं॥
primary_sources.transliteration:
savve pāṇā na hantavvā, na liṃhavvā na bandhavvā.
esā dhammo Mahāviro, ahiṃsā paramaṃ vrataṃ.
primary_sources.translation:
All living beings are not to be killed, not to be tormented, not to be bound.
This is the teaching of Mahāvīra: non‑violence is the supreme vow.
primary_sources.notes: The Ācārāṅga Sūtra is one of the earliest Śvetāmbara canonical texts and a key authority for Sthanakavasi Jains, who accept thirty‑two Āgamas. Its strong emphasis on ahiṃsā underlies Sthanakavasi critiques of practices that may involve harm, such as temple construction or ritual offerings. While the text does not explicitly discuss image‑worship, Sthanakavasi interpreters highlight its focus on conduct and restraint as evidence that inner discipline, rather than external ritual, is central to the Jain path.

primary_sources.title: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra
primary_sources.author: Traditionally attributed to early Jain teachers in the Śvetāmbara canon
primary_sources.original_text:
ण हन्तव्वं न लिंहव्वं, न बन्धव्वं न घातव्वं।
सव्वेसु पाणesu दया, एसा धम्मो जिणस्स य॥
primary_sources.transliteration:
ṇa hantavvaṃ na liṃhavvaṃ, na bandhavvaṃ na ghātavvaṃ.
savvesu pāṇesu dayā, esā dhammo jiṇassa ya.
primary_sources.translation:
One should not kill, not torment, not bind, not destroy.
Compassion toward all living beings—this indeed is the teaching of the Jina.
primary_sources.notes: The Uttarādhyayana Sūtra is widely used in Sthanakavasi svādhyāya and pratikramaṇa. Its verses on compassion and restraint are taken as foundational for both monastic and lay practice. Sthanakavasi teachers often cite such passages to argue that the heart of Jain religion lies in ethical discipline and compassion, not in external images or elaborate temple rituals.

primary_sources.title: Ṇamokāra (Navkār) Mantra
primary_sources.author: Canonical Jain prayer, not attributed to a single historical author
primary_sources.original_text:
णमो अरिहंताणं, णमो सिद्धाणं,
णमो आयरियाणं, णमो उवज्झायाणं,
णमो लोए सव्वसाहूणं॥
primary_sources.transliteration:
ṇamo arihaṃtāṇaṃ, ṇamo siddhāṇaṃ,
ṇamo āyariyāṇaṃ, ṇamo uvajjhāyāṇaṃ,
ṇamo loe savvasāhūṇaṃ.
primary_sources.translation:
Obeisance to the Arihants, obeisance to the Siddhas,
obeisance to the Ācāryas, obeisance to the Upādhyāyas,
obeisance to all Sādhus in the world.
primary_sources.notes: The Navkār Mantra is central to all Jain traditions, including Sthanakavasi. In Sthanakavasi practice, this mantra is recited without any accompanying image‑worship; the focus is on mentally contemplating the qualities of the Arihants, Siddhas, and teachers. This illustrates their emphasis on bhāva‑pūjā (inner worship) and supports their view that devotion does not require physical icons.

primary_sources.title: Pratikramaṇa liturgy (Śvetāmbara Sthanakavasi usage)
primary_sources.author: Composite liturgical tradition based on canonical and later texts
primary_sources.original_text:
मिच्छा मी दुक्कडं, सव्वे जिवा खमंतु मे।
खामेमि सव्वे जिवे, सव्वे जिवा खमंतु मे॥
primary_sources.transliteration:
micchā mī dukkadaṃ, savve jivā khamaṃtu me.
khāmemi savve jive, savve jivā khamaṃtu me.
primary_sources.translation:
May my faults be fruitless and bring no suffering; may all living beings forgive me.
I forgive all living beings; may all living beings forgive me.
primary_sources.notes: Daily and periodic pratikramaṇa is a core Sthanakavasi practice, performed in sthanak halls without images. The liturgy combines canonical phrases with later compositions, all oriented toward confession, forgiveness, and ethical renewal. This ritual exemplifies how Sthanakavasi communities structure their religious life around introspection and moral accountability rather than around offerings to images.

misconceptions.myth: Sthanakavasi Jains are completely separate from Śvetāmbara Jainism and follow a different basic doctrine.
misconceptions.reality: Sthanakavasi is a sub‑tradition within Śvetāmbara Jainism. Sthanakavasi Jains accept thirty‑two Śvetāmbara Āgamas and share the same core doctrines about the soul, karma, liberation, and ethical vows. Their main distinction lies in rejecting image‑worship and temple ritual, not in abandoning Śvetāmbara philosophy.

misconceptions.myth: Because they reject idols, Sthanakavasi Jains have very few rituals and a weak sense of devotion.
misconceptions.reality: Sthanakavasi practice is highly structured and devotional, but its focus is on inner worship, ethical discipline, and scriptural recitation. Daily pratikramaṇa, svādhyāya, meditation, and collective recitation of mantras like the Navkār are central. Their rejection of idols is not a rejection of devotion; it is a reorientation of devotion toward mental contemplation and conduct.

misconceptions.myth: Non‑idolatry in Sthanakavasi practice is simply a modern, rationalist reform with little basis in Jain scripture.
misconceptions.reality: Sthanakavasi non‑idolatry emerged from close study of the Jain Āgamas by figures such as Loṅkā Śāh, who argued that the canonical texts do not prescribe image‑worship or temple construction. Sthanakavasi teachers ground their stance in these scriptures and in the centrality of ahiṃsā and inner discipline, even though other Śvetāmbara groups interpret the same texts differently and accept image‑worship as a legitimate development.

misconceptions.myth: Sthanakavasi monks and nuns are less strict than other Jain mendicants because they do not practice extreme austerities like nudity.
misconceptions.reality: Sthanakavasi mendicants follow very rigorous disciplines: they wear simple white robes, use a mouth‑cloth at all times, eat only between sunrise and sunset, do not store food or water overnight, and limit their possessions to a few essential items. While their external austerities differ from those of Digambara monks, within the Śvetāmbara framework they are known for strict observance of vows and careful attention to non‑violence.
